Title: ESpeakTextAudioConverter - eSpeak TTS Implementation
Summary: ITextAudioConverter implementation that runs the eSpeak command-line TTS synthesizer and returns an empty WebViewAudioArtifact as a marker. eSpeak plays the synthesised speech directly to the default audio device — no IAudioPlayer is required. Internally serialises all calls through a SemaphoreSlim(1,1) to prevent concurrent eSpeak processes from fighting over the host audio device, which would otherwise cause clipped/cut-off audio when streaming sentences. Registered keyed-scoped under the key "espeak.tts".
Content:
## ESpeakTextAudioConverter

**Project**: Cyrena.Voice.Extension
**Type**: Internal class (implements public contract `ITextAudioConverter`)
**DI Key**: `ESpeakTextAudioConverter.Key` = `"espeak.tts"` (registered via `AddKeyedScoped<ITextAudioConverter, ESpeakTextAudioConverter>(ESpeakTextAudioConverter.Key)`)
**Namespace**: `Cyrena.Voice.Services`
**Target Framework**: .NET 10.0

---

### Purpose

Text-to-speech converter backed by the eSpeak command-line synthesizer.
Spawns `espeak` with the requested text on the command line and lets
eSpeak play the synthesised speech directly to the default audio device
on the host OS. The call returns an empty `WebViewAudioArtifact` as a
marker — the same pattern used by `WebViewTextAudioConverter`.

**No `IAudioPlayer` is required.** The user's audio output is whatever
eSpeak's audio device is configured to be (ALSA / PulseAudio / PipeWire on
Linux, the default audio endpoint on Windows). eSpeak's own playback
synchronisation handles the rest. This is the same fire-and-forget
pattern as the WebView converter, which lets the browser play the
synthesised audio via `speechSynthesis`.

---

### Concurrency: process-level serialisation

eSpeak plays directly to the host's default audio device. If two
`ConvertAsync` calls run concurrently — e.g. a `RunQueue` consumer
that dequeues sentences as fast as the streaming formatter produces
them — the second eSpeak process opens a fresh audio stream while the
first is still flushing. On PulseAudio/PipeWire (Linux) and the Windows
audio stack this manifests as **clipped/cut-off audio, overlapping
utterances, and dropped first words of each new sentence**.

To prevent this, every `ConvertAsync` call is serialised through an
instance-level `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)`. The gate is acquired before the
process starts and released in a `finally` after `WaitForExitAsync`
returns. Because `Process.WaitForExitAsync` reliably returns only after
the eSpeak process has fully exited and released its audio device, the
gate guarantees the next call does not start until the previous
utterance has finished playing.

The WebView converter is unaffected — it doesn't share this gate, since
the browser's `speechSynthesis` API handles its own queueing and audio
device arbitration internally.

`WaitAsync` honours the supplied `CancellationToken`, so cancelling an
in-flight call also lets the next call proceed (the gate is still
released in the `finally`).

---

### Public Surface

```csharp
namespace Cyrena.Voice.Services;

internal class ESpeakTextAudioConverter : ITextAudioConverter, IDisposable
{
    public const string Key = "espeak.tts";

    public ESpeakTextAudioConverter(ISettingsService settings);
    public bool IsInitialized { get; }

    public Task InitializeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
    public Task DeinitializeAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
    public void Dispose();
    public Task<AudioArtifact> ConvertAsync(string text, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
}
```

Implements `Cyrena.Voice.Contracts.ITextAudioConverter`. The lifecycle
pattern matches the rest of the voice pipeline:

```
[Created] → InitializeAsync() → [Operational] → DeinitializeAsync() → [Disposed]
```

`InitializeAsync` is a no-op (sets `IsInitialized = true`). There is no
session state to warm up — each `ConvertAsync` invocation is
self-contained.

`Dispose` also disposes the internal `SemaphoreSlim`.

---

### Configuration: ESpeakOptions

Configuration is read at the start of every `ConvertAsync` call via
`ISettingsService.Read<ESpeakOptions>(ESpeakOptions.Key)`. If no
settings have been persisted, a fresh `ESpeakOptions()` is used.

```csharp
namespace Cyrena.Voice.Options;

public class ESpeakOptions
{
    public const string Key = "espeak.tts";

    public string? BinaryPath { get; set; }   // null → "espeak" from PATH
    public string  Voice      { get; set; }   // default "en"
    public int     Speed      { get; set; }   // words per minute, default 175
    public int     Pitch      { get; set; }   // 0–99, default 50
    public int     Amplitude  { get; set; }   // 0–200, default 100
    public int     WordGap    { get; set; }   // 10 ms units, default 0
}
```

| Option | espeak flag | Notes |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| `BinaryPath` | (process start) | If null, the OS process launcher searches PATH for `espeak`. |
| `Voice` | `-v` | Run `espeak --voices=variant` to list available voices. |
| `Speed` | `-s` | Words per minute; eSpeak typically accepts ~80–500. |
| `Pitch` | `-p` | Pitch adjustment, 0–99. |
| `Amplitude` | `-a` | Volume, 0–200. |
| `WordGap` | `-g` | Pause between words in 10 ms units. Only emitted if `> 0`. |

Values outside eSpeak's accepted ranges are passed through unchanged
and will cause the underlying command to fail. Validation lives in
eSpeak itself.

---

### Process Invocation

The converter runs `Process` with `RedirectStandardError = true` (so
that any error message can be surfaced in the exception on a non-zero
exit) and `WaitForExitAsync` to block until the speech is done. The
process is registered with a `CancellationToken` callback that calls
`process.Kill(entireProcessTree: true)` so callers can abort an
in-flight utterance.

The command line is constructed as a single string, e.g.:

```
espeak -v en -s 175 -p 50 -a 100 'Hello, world!'
```

The text is wrapped in single quotes with embedded single quotes
escaped using the standard `'\''` sequence. This protects against
shell-style injection even though the process is launched with
`UseShellExecute = false` (the OS still interprets the final
`argv` array from this string).

**eSpeak playback behaviour**: eSpeak runs the entire utterance to
completion before exiting, so `WaitForExitAsync` returns only when the
speech is done. There is no streaming. If you need cancellable mid-
utterance behaviour, use the `CancellationToken` argument — the
converter kills the eSpeak process and throws
`OperationCanceledException`.

---

### Audio Output: WebViewAudioArtifact (marker)

```csharp
return new WebViewAudioArtifact();
```

`ConvertAsync` returns an empty `WebViewAudioArtifact` — the same
marker used by the WebView converter. The artifact exists so the
caller's `ITextAudioConverter` invocation returns *something*, but the
audio has already been played by eSpeak and the artifact carries no
audio data.

If `ConvertAsync` is called with null/whitespace input, the converter
returns `new WebViewAudioArtifact()` without taking the gate or
spawning eSpeak.

---

### Error Behavior

`ConvertAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException` when:

- The espeak binary cannot be located or started (wraps the underlying
  `Win32Exception`). Message includes the resolved binary path so the
  user can correct `ESpeakOptions.BinaryPath` or install eSpeak on PATH.
- The process exits with a non-zero code. Message includes captured
  stderr.

`OperationCanceledException` is thrown when the supplied
`CancellationToken` fires. The spawned eSpeak process is killed as
part of the cancellation callback, and the gate is released in the
`finally` so the next caller can proceed.

### DI Registration

```csharp
// In VoiceExtension.BuildExtension:
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<ITextAudioConverter, ESpeakTextAudioConverter>(
    ESpeakTextAudioConverter.Key);
```

Coexists with the WebView converter — both are keyed-scoped under their
own keys (`"webview.tts"` and `"espeak.tts"`). Consumers select via
`[FromKeyedServices("espeak.tts")] ITextAudioConverter` or by
building a `VoiceChain` that resolves the keyed instance.

Note: the converter is registered **scoped**, not singleton. Because
serialisation is implemented via an instance field, the gate only
protects calls that go through the same DI scope. In practice the
Toolbar resolves the converter once per `RunQueue` and never shares
it with concurrent scopes, so this is correct. If a future call site
needs cross-scope serialisation, the gate should be lifted to a
singleton or to `Cyrena.Voice.Core`.

---

### Lifecycle Notes

- **InitializeAsync**: sets `IsInitialized = true`. No process work.
- **DeinitializeAsync**: sets `IsInitialized = false`. No process work.
- **Dispose**: sets `IsInitialized = false` and disposes the
  `SemaphoreSlim`. The `IsInitialized` flag is informational; the
  contract does not require it to gate `ConvertAsync`.

---

### Differences from WebViewTextAudioConverter

| Aspect | WebView | ESpeak |
|--------|---------|--------|
| Mechanism | JS `speechSynthesis` (browser) | External `espeak` process |
| Audio location | Streamed to browser speakers immediately | Played to host audio device by eSpeak |
| Returns | `WebViewAudioArtifact` (marker) | `WebViewAudioArtifact` (marker) |
| Needs `IJSRuntime` | Yes | No |
| Needs `IAudioPlayer` | No | No |
| Needs process serialisation | No (browser handles it) | **Yes** (instance `SemaphoreSlim`) |
| Config source | `VoiceOptions` (browser voices) | `ESpeakOptions` (espeak binary + flags) |
| DI Key | `"webview.tts"` | `"espeak.tts"` |
| Cross-platform | Anywhere with a browser | Anywhere with `espeak` installed |

The two implementations now have the same contract shape: invoke →
play audio → return marker. They differ only in how audio is produced
(in-browser TTS vs. external process), what config schema they read,
and which (if any) serialisation is needed to avoid audio device
contention.

---

### Usage Example

```csharp
// In a VoiceChain implementation
public ITextAudioConverter Converter { get; }

// Constructor injection of the keyed instance
public MyChain(
    [FromKeyedServices(ESpeakTextAudioConverter.Key)] ITextAudioConverter converter)
{
    Converter = converter;
}

// Then at use time
var artifact = await Converter.ConvertAsync("Hello, world.", ct);
// eSpeak has already played the text; artifact is an empty WebViewAudioArtifact
```
